readThisFirst: Nothing in this file marks anybody. It is a set of drafts written so that the fourteen decisions in docs/teacher-review.md Part A arrive as something to approve or amend rather than something to author from scratch. data/rubrics.json and data/rubrics.draft.json are untouched by it and stay untouched until a human copies a proposal across by hand. scripts/check-proposals.mjs fails if any of these steps has already been copied into the live file, so an approved proposal cannot leave a ghost behind here that nobody notices.
source: Each proposal was written from the marking-scheme PDF under public/papers/ and the question paper beside it, read directly rather than from the summary in docs/teacher-review.md. Where CBSE printed a mark in its margin, the proposal uses CBSE's number and says so in cbsePrinted. Where CBSE printed only a total, the split is this file's judgment and iInferred says what it rests on.

howToRead.ref: the entry in docs/teacher-review.md Part A this answers
howToRead.kind: replace-steps — the rubric exists, the steps below would take the place of its steps; new-rubric — no rubric exists for this option, the whole object below would be added; confirm-as-is — no change proposed, and the reason is given
howToRead.todayAStudentLoses: who is mis-marked before the proposal
howToRead.cbsePrinted: what is in CBSE's margin. Not this file's to move.
howToRead.iInferred: everything else, and what it rests on
howToRead.teacherQuestion: what is still yours to settle, narrowed as far as it would go
howToRead.ifAdopted: who scores differently, and by how much
howToRead.proposed: for replace-steps, the fields that would change on the existing rubric; for new-rubric, the whole rubric. Shaped as data/rubrics.schema.md defines, so approving it is a copy and not a translation.

noteOnDiagrams: Several proposals below add a diagram step. Per data/rubrics.schema.md a diagram step is never auto-graded: it resolves to unmarked, with no colour, and waits for a person. So agreeing to a diagram mark is not agreeing that the machine will judge a drawing — it is reserving that mark for yourself, and accepting that the machine's top score on the question drops by that much. That is a different thing to agree to, and it is the thing being asked.

proposals.title: Science 2024-25 sample, Q34 option A — substitution, combustion, homologues
proposals.todayAStudentLoses: The rubric contains one thing: any two characteristics of a homologous series, at 2½ each. A student who justifies Keerthi, comments on methane and propane, draws the electron dot structure of ethane and answers the ethyne part — four of the five marks CBSE prints — and does not list two characteristics scores 0 out of 5.
proposals.cbsePrinted: Five separate (1)s down the margin of page 6 and the top of page 7: (1) against the Keerthi justification; (1) against methane and propane undergoing combustion; (1) against the electron dot structure of ethane; (1) against ANY TWO CHARACTERISTICS; (1) against the ethyne answer. The mark split of this question is entirely CBSE's. Nothing about the 5 is a judgment.
proposals.iInferred: Two things. First, that CBSE's single (1) against ANY TWO CHARACTERISTICS divides as ½ a characteristic — CBSE prints the 1 against the group and asks for two, and ½ each is the only division of 1 into 2 that CBSE's grain allows. Second, that 'Draw the electron dot structure of the immediate lower homologue of Propane' is a drawing, so its printed 1 becomes a diagram step and is reserved for a human rather than keyword-matched.
proposals.teacherQuestion: Two yes/no. (1) Half a mark per characteristic — yes or no? (2) Is the electron dot structure a drawing you want to mark yourself, or would you rather the machine accepted the written words 'ethane' or 'C2H6' for it? If the second, say so and the diagram step becomes an ordinary step.
proposals.ifAdopted: A student who answers (i), (ii) and (iii) and lists no characteristics goes from 0/5 to 4/5. A student who lists two characteristics and nothing else goes from 5/5 to 1/5. Because the electron-dot mark is reserved for a person, the machine's own ceiling on this question is 4 out of 5.

steps.awardFor: Keerthi is correct: substitution occurs in saturated hydrocarbons, where hydrogen atoms are replaced; unsaturated hydrocarbons undergo addition across the double or triple bond

partial.note: names Keerthi as correct but gives no reason, or gives the reason without saying whose thinking it supports

steps.awardFor: methane and propane undergo combustion in the presence of oxygen and release a large amount of energy

partial.note: says they burn but does not say that energy is released, or the reverse

steps.awardFor: correct electron dot structure of ethane, the immediate lower homologue of propane
any two characteristics of a homologous series

options.awardFor: successive members differ by a CH2 unit, that is by 14 u of molecular mass
all members share the same general formula and the same functional group
all members show similar chemical properties
physical properties change gradually along the series

steps.awardFor: ethyne with enough oxygen burns completely with a clean blue flame; with air, or with too little oxygen, combustion is incomplete and the flame is sooty

partial.note: names the sooty flame without saying why, or describes only the oxygen case

reviewNotes: Every mark here is CBSE's own: five (1)s printed down the margin of the scheme, page 6 and the top of page 7. Only the half plus half inside the characteristics group is this file's, and it is the only division of CBSE's 1 into two that a half-mark grain permits.

The electron dot structure is modelled as a diagram step, so its mark is never awarded automatically and waits for a human. That is not a mark CBSE reserved for a figure — CBSE prints (1) against it as it does against the prose — it is this file reading 'Draw the electron dot structure' in the stem as a drawing. A teacher who would rather the machine accepted the word 'ethane' should say so and this becomes an ordinary step.
Proposed by scripts/check-proposals.mjs's companion file data/rubric-proposals.json. No teacher has approved it.

proposals.title: Science 2024-25 sample, Q34 option B — cleansing action and saponification (the option nobody wrote up)
proposals.todayAStudentLoses: Every student who chose option B. There is nothing for their script to be marked against at all, so it comes back ungraded rather than wrong. This is the second problem docs/teacher-review.md raises under A1.
proposals.cbsePrinted: (1) against the choice of B with its reason; '(Labelled fig - 1 + 2)' against the cleansing-action part, so 1 for the micelle diagram and 2 for the explanation; '(0.5 + 0.5)' against the saponification part, so half for the equation and half for naming the process. 1 + 1 + 2 + ½ + ½ = 5. All of it printed.
proposals.iInferred: Only the wording of the concepts inside each step. The numbers are CBSE's, including the figure mark, which CBSE prints in so many words.
proposals.teacherQuestion: Is this accurate enough to use, so that a student who picks option B is graded rather than left ungraded? Yes or no.
proposals.ifAdopted: Students who chose option B stop coming back ungraded. The machine's ceiling on the option is 4 of 5, because CBSE itself puts 1 mark on the labelled micelle diagram and a machine never awards a drawing.

proposed.subject: Science
proposed.prompt: Attempt either option A or B. B. (i) 'A' and 'B' are sodium salts of a long-chain carboxylic acid and a long-chain sulphonic acid. Which would you prefer as a cleansing agent in hand-pump water, and why? (ii) Elaborate on the process of cleansing action; illustrate a micelle with a labelled diagram. (iii) Write the chemical equation for the preparation of soap from an ester, and name the process.

scheme.excerpt: B. (i) 'B' is preferred for cleansing action. The calcium and magnesium salts present in underground water are precipitated with carboxylic acids. The Ca++ and Mg++ salts of sulphonic acid are soluble in water. 'B' is a more effective cleansing agent in presence of Ca and Mg salts. (1) (ii) Soaps are molecules in which the two ends have differing properties, one is hydrophilic, that is, it dissolves in water, while the other end is hydrophobic. The soap molecules thus form structures called micelles where one end of the molecules is towards the oil droplet while the ionic end faces outside. This forms an emulsion in water. (Labelled fig - 1 + 2) (iii) CH3(CH2)16COOR + NaOH gives CH3(CH2)16COONa + ROH. The process is saponification. (0.5 + 0.5)

steps.awardFor: B, the sulphonic acid salt, because the calcium and magnesium salts of sulphonic acid stay soluble in hard water while those of carboxylic acid are precipitated

partial.note: picks B but gives no reason involving the calcium and magnesium salts

steps.awardFor: labelled diagram of a micelle

a soap molecule has a hydrophilic ionic end and a hydrophobic hydrocarbon end; the tails turn in towards the oil and the ionic heads face the water, forming micelles that carry the dirt away as an emulsion

partial.note: describes the two ends of the soap molecule but never reaches the micelle, or names the micelle with no account of the two ends

steps.awardFor: the equation: the ester plus sodium hydroxide gives the sodium salt of the acid and an alcohol
names the process: saponification

reviewNotes: Every mark is CBSE's own, printed on page 7 of the scheme: (1), then '(Labelled fig - 1 + 2)', then '(0.5 + 0.5)'. Nothing was divided by this file.
CBSE prints the figure mark here in so many words, so the micelle is a diagram step and is never awarded automatically. The machine's ceiling on this option is 4 of 5.
Saponification is a specific term, so acceptEquivalentWording is off on that step and a near miss should not be green.

The schema carries "or equivalent wording" as one flag for the whole rubric, not per step. Saponification is an answer that must be exact, so a grader must not accept a near miss there even though the rubric-wide flag is on. If that cannot be honoured, turn the rubric-wide flag off and accept that the prose steps become stricter too.
This rubric has never been read by a teacher. It is proposed, not approved.

proposals.title: Science 2015-16 sample, Q21 — speciation, the gene, the hair-colour cross
proposals.todayAStudentLoses: The rubric is a single 'any two of' group worth 2½ each, and the two things it will accept are the definition of a gene and the hair-colour cross. So the speciation part — which is what the group is labelled after — earns nothing, and a student who names migration and mutation and stops scores 0 out of 5. Conversely a student who defines a gene and does the cross scores a full 5 without ever mentioning speciation.
proposals.cbsePrinted: Six numbers down the margin of page 4, read off by line position rather than by text order. 1 sits level with 'A. Speciation may take place by'. 1 sits level with the second line of the gene definition. ½ sits level with 'Red hair – Mother – Recessive so bb'. ½ sits level with 'Black hair – father Dominant so BB'. 1 sits level with the 'Father Mother' row of the cross. 1 sits level with the 'F1 Bb (Black)' row. 1 + 1 + ½ + ½ + 1 + 1 = 5.
proposals.iInferred: That CBSE's single 1 against part A divides as half a mark per speciation mechanism, since the scheme asks for any two and 1 splits into two halves and nothing else. Also, that the conclusion 'the child will have black hair' is carried by the F1 mark rather than being a seventh unmarked line — the margin prints nothing against it and there is no mark left over.
proposals.teacherQuestion: One number and one confirmation. (1) Part A gets 1 mark for two mechanisms — half a mark each — yes or no? (2) The margin alignment above is the whole basis for the split; if you read the column differently, write the six numbers you would use.
proposals.ifAdopted: A student who names two mechanisms and stops goes from 0/5 to 1/5. A student who defines the gene and works the cross correctly and skips speciation goes from 5/5 to 4/5. A student who does everything scores 5 either way. The scoring stops depending on which two of the three parts happened to be answered.

steps.awardFor: any two ways speciation takes place
defines a gene as a functional segment of DNA

partial.note: names DNA but does not say the gene is a functional segment of it

steps.awardFor: the mother carries red hair, which is recessive, so her contribution is b
the father carries black hair, which is dominant, so his contribution is B
sets out the cross of the two parents
the F1 child is Bb and therefore has black hair, because black is dominant

partial.note: reaches Bb but never states the hair colour, or states black with no genotype behind it

reviewNotes: The six marks are CBSE's own column on page 4 of the scheme, read off by line position: 1 against part A, 1 against the gene definition, half and half against the two parental genotypes, 1 against the parental cross, 1 against the F1 result.
The half plus half inside the speciation group is this file's, not CBSE's: CBSE prints one 1 against a list it asks two items from, and 1 divides into two halves and nothing else at CBSE's grain.
Science 2016-17 Q21 is the same question with the same scheme page. Whatever is decided here should be applied there unchanged.
Proposed. No teacher has approved it.

proposals.title: Science 2022-23 practice paper, Q33 — ozone formation, ground-level ozone, health consequences
proposals.todayAStudentLoses: The rubric holds only part (c), at 1½ per consequence, and one of its three options is the scheme's instruction line rather than an answer, so the word 'consequences' scores 1½ on its own. A student who explains the formation of ozone and why ground-level ozone is a pollutant — 2 of the 3 marks CBSE prints — and names no health consequence scores 0 out of 3.
proposals.cbsePrinted: All three marks, in words rather than in a margin: '(a) 0.5 marks for each correct point' over two points; '(b) Ozone is deadly to humans at lower levels of the atmosphere. [1 mark]'; '(c) 0.5 marks each for any two consequences'. ½ + ½ + 1 + ½ + ½ = 3.
proposals.iInferred: Nothing about the marks. Only which extra consequences to list beyond CBSE's two, since the scheme says 'Accept any other valid answer' and names only skin cancer and cataract. I have added weakened immunity and sunburn or premature ageing of the skin.
proposals.teacherQuestion: One yes/no: are 'weakened immune system' and 'sunburn or premature ageing of the skin' acceptable alongside skin cancer and cataract? If not, strike them and the group falls back to CBSE's two.
proposals.ifAdopted: A student who answers (a) and (b) and gives no consequence goes from 0/3 to 2/3. A student who writes only the word 'consequences' goes from 1½/3 to 0. Full answers score 3 either way.

steps.awardFor: high-energy UV radiation from the Sun breaks molecular oxygen into free oxygen atoms
the free oxygen combines with molecular oxygen to form ozone
at ground level ozone is a pollutant because it is deadly to humans — it is poisonous in the lower atmosphere

partial.note: says ozone is harmful without tying the harm to the lower atmosphere, so the contrast the question turns on is missing

steps.awardFor: any two health consequences of ozone depletion

options.awardFor: sunburn or premature ageing of the skin

reviewNotes: Every mark is CBSE's own, printed in words on page 5 of the scheme: half plus half for (a), 1 for (b), half plus half for (c). Nothing was divided by this file.

Options o3 and o4 in the consequences group are not CBSE's. The scheme lists skin cancer and cataract and adds 'Accept any other valid answer'; these two are this file's reading of that licence and a teacher may strike them.
The two half-mark steps carry no partial rule, because CBSE has no quarter mark: a half-mark step is green or it is red.
Proposed. No teacher has approved it.

proposals.title: Mathematics (Standard) 2022-23 sample, Q30 option A — the parallelogram circumscribing a circle
proposals.todayAStudentLoses: Nothing structural — the four marks are CBSE's own and they sum correctly. What is wrong is the keywords: step 2 is satisfied by the single word 'adding', and step 1 by the word 'circle'. A student who writes 'adding the circle' scores 2 of 3.
proposals.cbsePrinted: Four numbers down the margin of page 5: 1 against the block that names the tangent points and writes the four equal-tangent pairs; 1 against 'AB+CD=AD+BC'; ½ against 'AB=DC and AD=BC (opposite sides of parallelogram)'; ½ against the conclusion. 1 + 1 + ½ + ½ = 3. No figure mark anywhere in the column — and the scheme's own page sets its text around a drawn figure while still paying nothing for it.
proposals.iInferred: Only the concepts inside each step. The proposal below adds no figure mark, on the strength of that margin.
proposals.teacherQuestion: One yes/no, and it is the real one: the paper supplies no figure here, so the candidate must draw and label one to write this proof at all. If you also take the figure mark: a student who draws a correct labelled figure and writes a short proof gains half a mark, and the machine's ceiling on the question falls to 2½ of 3, because a drawing waits for a person.

proposals.title: Mathematics (Standard) 2022-23 sample, Q30 option B — the angle between two parallel tangents (the option nobody wrote up)
proposals.todayAStudentLoses: Everyone who took the OR. Their script has nothing to be marked against and comes back ungraded. This is the second problem docs/teacher-review.md raises under A5.
proposals.cbsePrinted: Five numbers down the margin of page 6: 1 against the block joining OC and setting up the two triangles with OP = OC, PA = CA and AO common; ½ against the SSS congruency; ½ against angle 1 = angle 2 by CPCT and likewise angle 3 = angle 4; ½ against the co-interior angles being supplementary; ½ against 2 angle 2 + 2 angle 4 = 180 degrees, so angle 2 + angle 4 = 90 degrees. 1 + ½ + ½ + ½ + ½ = 3.
proposals.iInferred: Only the concepts inside each step, and that the final line 'angle AOB = 90 degrees' is carried by the last half mark rather than being unmarked — the column prints nothing beside it and there is no mark left over.
proposals.teacherQuestion: Is this accurate enough to use, so that a student who took the OR is graded rather than left ungraded? Yes or no. The figure here is printed on the question paper, so no drawing mark arises.
proposals.ifAdopted: Students who chose option B stop coming back ungraded, and the question becomes fully machine-markable — nothing on this option sits on a drawing.

proposed.subject: Mathematics
proposed.prompt: In the figure XY and X'Y' are two parallel tangents to a circle with centre O and another tangent AB with point of contact C intersecting XY at A and X'Y' at B. What is the measure of angle AOB?

scheme.excerpt: Join OC. In Δ OPA and Δ OCA: OP = OC (radii of same circle); PA = CA (length of two tangents from an external point); AO = AO (Common) (1). Therefore Δ OPA congruent Δ OCA (By SSS congruency criterion) (half). Hence angle 1 = angle 2 (CPCT); Similarly angle 3 = angle 4 (half). angle PAB + angle QBA = 180 (co interior angles are supplementary as XY parallel X'Y') (half). 2 angle 2 + 2 angle 4 = 180; angle 2 + angle 4 = 90 (half). angle 2 + angle 4 + angle AOB = 180 (Angle sum property). Using (1), we get angle AOB = 90

steps.awardFor: joins OC and sets up the two triangles: OP = OC as radii, PA = CA as tangents from an external point, AO common

partial.note: sets up the triangles but omits one of the three equalities the congruence rests on

steps.awardFor: concludes that the two triangles are congruent by SSS
angle 1 = angle 2 by CPCT, and similarly angle 3 = angle 4
the two angles at A and B sum to 180 degrees, because XY parallel to X'Y' makes them co-interior
halving gives angle 2 + angle 4 = 90 degrees, so by the angle sum property angle AOB = 90 degrees

reviewNotes: Every mark is CBSE's own column on page 6 of the scheme: 1 + half + half + half + half = 3.
The four half-mark steps carry no partial rule, because a half-mark step cannot be partially credited at CBSE's grain: it is green or it is red.
The figure is printed on the question paper, so no diagram step arises.

The schema carries "or equivalent wording" as one flag for the whole rubric, not per step. The 90 degrees in the final step is an answer that must be exact, so a grader must not accept a near miss there even though the rubric-wide flag is on. If that cannot be honoured, turn the rubric-wide flag off and accept that the prose steps become stricter too.
This rubric has never been read by a teacher. It is proposed, not approved.

proposals.title: Science 2025-26 sample, Q13 — Draw and explain how the nerve cells help in transmission of impulses
proposals.todayAStudentLoses: Nobody is scored zero for a right answer here. The complaint is the opposite one: 1 of the 3 marks is reserved for a figure CBSE never paid for, and because a machine never awards a drawing, every student's machine total on this question is capped at 2 out of 3 — including a perfect script.

proposals.iInferred: All of it. The proposal is 1 mark per bullet, following the scheme's own three bullets, and no figure mark — which is a change to the live file, and the only proposal in this set that takes a mark away from somewhere rather than putting one back.
proposals.teacherQuestion: One yes/no, and this is the one to be most sceptical of. CBSE printed three marks over three prose bullets and paid nothing for a drawing. Do you follow the scheme — 1 + 1 + 1, fully machine-markable — or does 'Draw' in the stem earn the student a mark you will mark yourself? proposals.ifAdopted: A student who writes all three stages goes from a capped 2/3 to 3/3. A student who draws a correct labelled neuron and writes little goes from a reserved mark to nothing. The question stops dragging the accuracy test downwards.

steps.awardFor: information is detected at the specialised dendritic tip of a nerve cell and sets off a chemical reaction that creates an electrical impulse

partial.note: names the dendritic tip and the impulse but not the chemical reaction that generates it

steps.awardFor: the impulse travels from the dendrite to the cell body and then along the axon to its end, where it triggers the release of chemicals

partial.note: traces the impulse along the axon but never reaches the release of chemicals at its end

steps.awardFor: the chemicals cross the gap, or synapse, and start a similar impulse in a dendrite of the next neuron

reviewNotes: CBSE prints one total of 3 for the whole answer and nothing per step, so this 1 + 1 + 1 is inferred. What it rests on is the scheme's own body: three bullets, three marks, one mark a bullet.

This proposal removes the figure mark the live rubric reserves. CBSE prints no figure mark here — its (Fig. a) and (Fig b) are illustrations inside its prose, not marks in its column — and the reserved mark caps every machine total on this question at 2 of 3. The cost is that a student who draws a correct labelled neuron and writes little now scores nothing for the drawing. That is the trade, and it is the teacher's to take or refuse.
This is the only proposal in this file that takes a mark away from a student rather than restoring one. Read it twice.
Proposed. No teacher has approved it.

proposals.title: Social Science 2023-24 practice set 2, Q37 — the map question
proposals.todayAStudentLoses: Everyone. The rubric's two steps match on the words of the question rather than on any answer: step 1 is satisfied by the word 'India' and step 2 by the words 'Jallianwala Bagh' — which are not answers to this paper's question at all. A student who names both places correctly and marks all three symbols may match neither step.
proposals.cbsePrinted: The section heading itself: 'MAP SKILL-BASED QUESTION (2+3=5)', and 2 and 3 again in the margin against parts (a) and (b). So 2 for identifying and naming the two marked places, 3 for locating and labelling any three of the four listed items with suitable symbols.
proposals.iInferred: Two things, and the second is serious. First, that CBSE's 2 for part (a) divides 1 per place, and its 3 for part (b) 1 per item — the only division its own counts allow. Second, and this is the one to look at: the marking scheme prints answers that do not belong to this question paper. The paper asks for the place associated with the peasant satyagraha in Gujarat and for the Congress session of December 1920; the scheme answers Madras for a 1927 session, and Amritsar for the Jallianwala Bagh. CBSE has printed another set's answers on this page. The proposal therefore uses the paper's own answers — Kheda and Nagpur — and those two names are mine, not CBSE's.
proposals.teacherQuestion: Two. (1) Are Kheda and Nagpur the answers to this paper's A and B — yes or no? I am confident, but the printed scheme contradicts me and it is not my contradiction to resolve. (2) Part (b) is a cross on an outline of India: modelled below as a drawing worth 3, which no machine will ever award. Confirm that, or say that a name written beside the symbol should earn it instead — CBSE prints exactly that alternative for visually impaired candidates on the same page, so the wording already exists if you want it.
proposals.ifAdopted: Students stop being scored on whether they happened to write the word 'India'. Part (a) becomes markable — 2 of the 5. Part (b)'s 3 marks wait for a person, so the machine's ceiling on this question is 2 of 5, and honestly so: it cannot see where a cross was put.

steps.awardFor: place A — the place associated with the peasant satyagraha in Gujarat: Kheda
place B — the Indian National Congress session of December 1920: Nagpur
locates and labels any three of the four listed items on the outline map with suitable symbols
labels: Pune — a software technology park in Maharashtra
Bokaro — a coal mine in Jharkhand
Haldia — a seaport in West Bengal
Tehri Dam — the tallest dam in India

reviewNotes: The 2 and the 3 are CBSE's own, printed in the section heading (2+3=5) and again in the margin of page 17. The 1 plus 1 inside part (a), and the treatment of part (b) as a single drawing worth 3, are this file's.

The names Kheda and Nagpur are NOT from the marking scheme. The scheme on page 17 answers a different pair of clues from the ones this paper's Q37 prints — it gives Madras and Amritsar against questions about a 1927 session and the Jallianwala Bagh, where the paper asks about a Gujarat peasant satyagraha and the December 1920 session. CBSE appears to have printed another set's answers. Kheda and Nagpur are the answers to the questions actually asked, and they are this file's, not CBSE's. This is the one place in this file where a proposal contradicts the printed scheme, and it must not be signed off without a teacher agreeing to that.

Part (b) is modelled as a single diagram step worth 3, so it is never awarded automatically. It is not that a machine marks the map badly; it cannot see a pencil cross on an outline of India at all. The same page prints a name-only version of part (b) for visually impaired candidates, which is the alternative if a written answer is to be accepted instead.
acceptEquivalentWording is off: these are place names, and a near miss is not the place.
Proposed. No teacher has approved it.

proposals.title: Mathematics (Standard) 2022-23 sample, Q23 — the angle AQB from the tangents at P
proposals.todayAStudentLoses: Nothing to do with a figure — that warning is the false alarm the review page suspected. proposals.cbsePrinted: Three numbers down the margin of page 2: ½ against the two right angles between radius and tangent; ½ against the angle at the centre being 105 degrees; 1 against the answer 52.5 degrees. ½ + ½ + 1 = 2.
proposals.iInferred: Only the concepts inside each step, and two partial rules on the last: that a candidate who quotes the centre-angle rule and slips arithmetically keeps half, and that a right value with no degree sign keeps half. Both are mine.
proposals.teacherQuestion: Two, both quick. (1) The paper prints the figure — the stem opens 'In the given figure, O is the centre of the circle' — so no drawing mark arises. Confirm in one line. (2) Should an arithmetic slip in the last step keep half a mark, or is 52.5 all or nothing?
proposals.ifAdopted: The numbers finally have to be right. A student who writes the word 'angle' and no working goes from 2/2 to 0. A student who does the geometry correctly scores 2 as before.

steps.awardFor: the two angles at the points of contact are 90 degrees, because the radius is perpendicular to the tangent there
the angle at the centre AOB is 105 degrees, by the angle sum property
AQB is half of 105, that is 52.5 degrees, because the angle at the remaining part of the circle is half the angle the arc subtends at the centre

partial.note: quotes the centre-angle rule and halves 105 but the number that comes out is wrong
52.5 is right, the degree sign is absent

reviewNotes: The three marks are CBSE's own column on page 2 of the scheme: half + half + 1 = 2.

No diagram step. The question paper prints the figure — the stem opens 'In the given figure, O is the centre of the circle' — so the candidate draws nothing and the automatic drawing warning on this rubric is a false alarm.

The two partial rules on the final step are this file's, not CBSE's. Both are legal only because that step is worth a whole mark; the two half-mark steps above it are green or red with nothing in between.
Keywords have been split into real concepts and the three numbers are now checked for. Under the draft, the bare word 'angle' satisfied all three steps.

The schema carries "or equivalent wording" as one flag for the whole rubric, not per step. 52.5 is an answer that must be exact, so a grader must not accept a near miss there even though the rubric-wide flag is on. If that cannot be honoured, turn the rubric-wide flag off and accept that the prose steps become stricter too.
Proposed. No teacher has approved it.

proposed.subject: Mathematics
proposed.prompt: A solid sphere of radius 3 cm is melted and then recast into small spherical balls each of diameter 0.6 cm. Find the number of balls.

proposed.subject: Mathematics
proposed.prompt: The frequency distribution table of agriculture holdings in a village is given — area of land in hectares 1-3, 3-5, 5-7, 7-9, 9-11, 11-13 against 20, 45, 80, 55, 40 and 12 families. Find the modal agriculture holdings of the village.

scheme.excerpt: Modal class 5 - 7, with f0 = 45, f1 = 80, f2 = 55 (1). Modal class = 5 - 7, l = 5, h = 2. Mode = l + ((f1 - f0)/(2f1 - f0 - f2)) h = 5 + ((80 - 45)/(2(80) - 45 - 55)) 2 = 6.166. Hence, modal agriculture holdings of the village is 6.17 hectare (approx.) (2)

steps.awardFor: identifies 5-7 as the modal class, and reads off l = 5, h = 2, f1 = 80, f0 = 45, f2 = 55

partial.note: picks the modal class but does not read off the values the formula needs

steps.awardFor: substitutes into the mode formula and reaches 6.17 hectares, approximately

partial.note: quotes the mode formula and never substitutes the values into it
substitutes correctly and the number that comes out is wrong
